The coffee had gone cold twice before Mara noticed the clock on the wall was running backward—not broken, not stuck, but deliberately, smoothly reversing, as if time itself had decided to reconsider the morning. She blinked, certain sleep still clung to her eyes, but when she glanced down at her own hands, the faint scar on her knuckle from a childhood bicycle accident had vanished, only to reappear a heartbeat later when she blinked again. The apartment around her flickered between versions of itself: the peeling wallpaper from her twenties, the fresh paint of last spring, the moving boxes she hadn't yet unpacked. Somewhere between one breath and the next, Mara understood with a cold, electric certainty that she was no longer moving through time in the way everyone else was—she was slipping through it, like a thread pulled loose from the fabric of an ordinary Tuesday, and there was no telling yet whether she'd ever find her way back to the right moment, or if she even wanted to.
